text: Your baby may say 1-3 words with meaning by now. Celebrate every attempt at communication, even if the pronunciation is not perfect.
Walking may still be unsteady, and that is completely normal. Give your baby plenty of safe, open space to practice without shoes when possible.
Your baby may start bringing you objects to show you. This "joint attention" is a key milestone in social development and communication.
Try giving simple one-step directions like "bring me the cup." Even if they don't follow through, they are learning to understand language.
Your baby may enjoy scribbling with chunky crayons. The goal is not art but practicing grip and arm control.
Stacking 2-3 blocks is a common milestone around this age. It takes impressive coordination and concentration for little hands.
Your baby likely understands far more words than they can say. Keep narrating your day together to build their receptive vocabulary.
Pointing at pictures in books and looking at you for a response shows your baby is learning to share experiences. Name what they point to.
Imitation play becomes more complex now. Your baby may pretend to talk on a phone or stir food in a pot, copying what they see you do.
If your baby is not yet walking independently, they may be a proficient cruiser or crawler. Children develop gross motor skills on their own timeline.
Your baby may start showing preferences for certain toys, people, or activities. This developing personality is wonderful to watch unfold.
Encourage your baby to help with simple tasks like putting a toy in a basket. This builds a sense of capability and cooperation.
Your baby may shake their head "no" with gusto. This is an exciting sign that they understand and can express their own will.
Let your baby try feeding themselves with a spoon, even though most food will not make it to their mouth. Practice is more important than neatness.
Reading together for even 10 minutes daily has a powerful impact on language development. Let your baby choose the book and set the pace.
Many babies transition from two naps to one nap between 12 and 18 months. Signs of readiness include consistently fighting the morning nap.
When moving to one nap, shift the remaining nap to around 12:30-1 PM. An earlier bedtime can help bridge the gap during the transition.
Your baby still needs about 11-14 hours of total sleep per day. If nighttime sleep shortens, check that the daytime nap is not too long or too late.
New walking skills can cause temporary sleep disruptions as your baby processes these exciting motor developments during sleep.
Consistency matters more than perfection. If you miss a nap window or bedtime, simply get back on track the next day without stress.
If your baby wakes at night and calls for you, a brief and boring check-in is usually best. Keep lights off and your voice calm and quiet.
Consider introducing a consistent pre-nap routine of 5-10 minutes. A shortened version of the bedtime routine helps signal that sleep is coming.
Separation anxiety may peak again around 12-15 months. A calm, loving goodbye at bedtime with a consistent phrase helps your baby feel secure.
If your baby has just started walking, extra physical activity during the day can actually improve nighttime sleep quality.
Avoid screen time in the hour before bed. The blue light and stimulation can make it harder for your baby to wind down.
A comfort object like a small soft blanket or stuffed animal can help your baby self-soothe at this age. Keep it in the crib only for sleep.
The nap transition period can take 2-4 weeks. Some days your baby may need two naps and others just one. Follow their cues.
If your baby is in daycare, try to align your home sleep schedule with their daycare nap time for consistency.
A too-late bedtime can cause early morning waking. If your baby is up before 6 AM, try moving bedtime 15-30 minutes earlier.
Growth spurts can temporarily increase sleep needs. If your baby is suddenly sleeping more, they may be going through a physical growth phase.
Your baby can now transition to whole cow's milk if you are weaning from breast milk or formula. Aim for about {{16-24 ounces|475-710 ml}} per day.
If you haven't already, work toward weaning off the bottle. Offer milk in a straw cup or open cup at mealtimes to help with the transition.
Picky eating often begins around this age. Continue offering a variety of foods without pressure, and trust your baby's appetite.
Offer food from all food groups throughout the day: grains, protein, fruits, vegetables, and dairy. Variety across the week matters more than any single meal.
Your baby may eat a lot one day and almost nothing the next. This is normal. Their appetite self-regulates over time.
Serve the same meal to the whole family when possible. Your baby learns eating habits by watching you and will feel included.
Healthy fats from avocado, nut butters, olive oil, and full-fat dairy are essential for your baby's brain development at this age.
If your baby throws food on the floor, they may be telling you they are full or experimenting with gravity. Try smaller portions on the plate.
Let your baby practice using a spoon and fork. Pre-load the spoon for them if needed and choose utensils with short, chunky handles.

Limit juice to no more than {{4 ounces|120 ml}} of 100% fruit juice per day, if any. Whole fruits provide fiber and nutrition without the concentrated sugar. Water and milk are the best drink options.
If you are still breastfeeding alongside solids, that is wonderful. Nurse on demand and let your baby lead the gradual weaning process.
Offer new foods alongside familiar favorites. Your baby is more likely to try something new when it appears next to a food they already enjoy.
Mealtimes should last about 15-20 minutes. If your baby loses interest, let them leave the table rather than forcing them to stay.
Nut butters are a great protein source but should be spread thinly on toast or mixed into oatmeal, not given by the spoonful, to prevent choking.
Your baby's stomach is about the size of their fist. What looks like a tiny portion to you may be a full meal for them.
Your baby may be due for important vaccine boosters during this stage. Check with your pediatrician to make sure immunizations are on track, and use the visit to discuss growth and development.
Now that your baby is walking, minor bumps and bruises are inevitable. Keep a first aid kit accessible and know when a head bump needs medical attention.
Brush your baby's teeth twice a day with a small smear of fluoride toothpaste. Make it fun by letting them hold their own toothbrush too.
Hand, foot, and mouth disease is common in this age group. Watch for mouth sores, rash on hands and feet, and fever. It usually resolves on its own.
If your baby is in group childcare, expect more frequent colds. Each illness strengthens their immune system, even though it is exhausting in the moment.
Constipation can happen as your baby eats more solids. Offer high-fiber foods like pears, prunes, oatmeal, and plenty of water.
Your baby's first molars may be coming in around now, causing extra drooling and fussiness. Chilled washcloths and teething rings can help.
If your baby is not saying any words yet, mention it at the 15-month visit. Early intervention for speech delays is highly effective.
Keep your baby's nails trimmed short to prevent scratching. A good time to trim is right after a bath when nails are soft.
Children over 1 year need 600 IU of vitamin D daily. If your toddler does not drink enough fortified milk or get regular sun exposure, ask your pediatrician about a supplement.
If your baby has recurring ear infections, discuss with your pediatrician whether ear tubes might be beneficial.
Watch for signs of allergic reactions when introducing new foods: hives, swelling, vomiting, or difficulty breathing. Seek emergency help for severe reactions.
Your baby does not need shoes indoors. Barefoot time strengthens foot muscles and improves balance for new walkers.
Croup, with its characteristic barky cough, is common in the second year. Cool night air or steam from a hot shower can help ease symptoms.
Your baby should see a dentist by their first birthday or within six months of their first tooth. If you have already had that first visit, continue with check-ups every six months.
Give your baby a bucket and some balls or blocks to practice dropping objects in and dumping them out. Repetitive play is how they master new skills.
Try finger painting with edible paints made from yogurt or mashed fruit. It is messy but wonderful for sensory development.
Walk together outside and let your baby set the pace. Stopping to examine every leaf and pebble is exactly how they learn about the world.
Push and pull toys are perfect for new walkers. They add fun to walking practice and help with balance and coordination.
Read lift-the-flap books together. The surprise element keeps your baby engaged and teaches them about hidden objects.
Create a sensory bin with dried pasta, large scoops, and cups. Supervise closely and choose pieces too large to be a choking risk.
Your baby may love helping with household tasks. Give them a small cloth to "wipe" surfaces or let them stir something in a bowl.
Build a tower of blocks and let your baby knock it down, then encourage them to stack one or two blocks themselves.
Play simple chase games like "I'm going to get you!" Running and changing direction builds agility and brings lots of laughter.
Offer shape sorters with just 2-3 simple shapes to start. Show your baby how one shape fits and let them try the rest.
Sandbox play with scoops and molds is a wonderful outdoor activity. Digging and pouring develop hand strength and coordination.
Play pretend with a toy phone or doll. Simple pretend play is emerging at this age and supports cognitive development.
Blow bubbles and let your baby try to catch or pop them. This is great for visual tracking and gross motor coordination.
Create a low climbing area with firm cushions or a step stool. Supervised climbing builds strength, balance, and confidence.
Name animals and their sounds while looking at picture books. Your baby may start imitating animal sounds before using many real words.
Now that your baby can walk, re-check your babyproofing from their new height. They can reach countertops, table edges, and door handles more easily.
Keep your baby rear-facing in their car seat as long as possible, until your child reaches the maximum height or weight limit of the seat. Rear-facing is the safest position for young children.
Never leave your baby alone near any body of water, including bathtubs, wading pools, and buckets. Active supervision means eyes on them at all times.
Secure heavy appliances like TVs and microwaves. A walking baby who pulls on cords can bring them crashing down.
Keep hot drinks and plates away from table edges. A walking baby can reach up and pull things down in an instant.
Use stove knob covers and keep pot handles turned inward when cooking. Curious hands can reach the stove sooner than you expect.
Lock all doors leading to garages, basements, and outdoor areas. Your baby is fast and can slip through an open door in seconds.
Avoid hard, round, or sticky foods that are common choking hazards: whole grapes, popcorn, hard candy, chunks of raw carrot, and large globs of nut butter.
Check that all houseplants are non-toxic. Babies at this age put everything in their mouths and may grab leaves from low-sitting plants.
Use door stoppers or door finger guards to prevent your baby from pinching their fingers in closing doors.
If you have a pool or pond, install a four-sided fence with a self-closing, self-latching gate. Fencing is the single most effective drowning prevention.
Keep magnets, especially small high-powered ones, completely away from your baby. Swallowed magnets can cause life-threatening internal injuries.
Always hold your baby's hand in parking lots and near roads. They do not yet understand traffic danger and can dart away quickly.
Review your baby's car seat harness fit regularly. The chest clip should be at armpit level and straps should be snug with no slack.
Store pet food and water bowls out of reach. Baby-safe does not mean baby-appropriate, and pet food can be a choking hazard.
